title: Evaluating a Generate–Validate–Repair Pipeline for LLM‑based Network Configuration: a Paired, Emulation‑Grounded Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, emulation‑grounded experiment (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) to test whether adding a deterministic network verifier to a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline reduces unsafe configuration applications from an LLM relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. Using N = 240 paired intents (144 in‑distribution, 48 distribution‑shift, 48 adversarial) under shared_initial_candidate semantics (one initial LLM generation per task reused across paired arms), the run completed as planned (planned episodes = 480, completed = 480, hosted_model_call_event_count = 240, model_calls_used = 240). Every paired episode was scored safe under both arms: baseline = 240/240 = 1.0, guarded = 240/240 = 1.0; paired difference = 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.00]; bootstrap resamples = 10,000, seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. No validator‑triggered repairs were applied because every shared initial candidate passed the deterministic validator. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics the paired contrast can only differ if the shared initial candidate fails validation or if a validator‑triggered repair is applied; we state this constraint explicitly in Abstract and Conclusion and map archived 'success' fields to the preregistered unsafe_apply/safe_apply estimand. We present the preregistered design, exact execution accounting, artifact‑grounded analysis, and a failure‑analytic interpretation of the null paired outcome together with artifact‑based recommendations for future emulation‑grounded NetOps evaluations.

sections.introduction:
LLM‑based tools are increasingly proposed to translate operator intent into device configurations and to automate routine NetOps workflows. Execution‑grounded evaluations that embed LLM agents into emulated networks expose failure modes that token‑level measures miss: planning errors, ordering violations, and workflow‑level semantic faults can produce unsafe device states even when generated commands are syntactically correct [1]. A recurring mitigation pattern is generate–validate–repair (GVR): produce a candidate configuration with an LLM, run a deterministic validator that checks intent and workflow invariants, and invoke a repair routine when the validator flags violations [2,3].

We preregistered and executed a paired, emulation‑grounded experiment to quantify whether adding a deterministic verifier (with at most one validator‑triggered repair) reduces the rate of unsafe configuration applications from an LLM relative to an LLM‑only pipeline when the same initial LLM candidate is shared across paired arms. Our contributions are: (1) a fully preregistered paired confirmatory run and complete execution accounting (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01); (2) artifact‑grounded reporting of exact per‑call traces and analysis artifacts that map to the preregistered estimand; and (3) a failure‑analytic interpretation of a null paired outcome with concrete, artifact‑supported recommendations for future paired GVR evaluations.
sections.related_work: Executable, emulation‑grounded benchmarks and closed‑loop agent evaluations have been proposed to stress multi‑step NetOps tasks and to detect planning/execution faults that text‑only evaluations miss [1]. Recent work on automated configuration repair and program repair documents generate–validate or generate–validate–repair patterns and reports improved syntactic and limited semantic repair coverage when validators provide actionable failure signals [2,4]. Position and survey papers emphasize tool augmentation (verifiers, knowledge graphs), uncertainty calibration, and layered defenses for agentic systems, while noting unresolved empirical questions about verifier benefit under distribution shift and adversarial prompts [3,5]. Practical NetOps evaluation requires emulation, hidden executable tests, and deterministic offline scoring to measure operational safety; NetConfArena and similar benchmarks provide one executable design point but do not yet resolve broader external‑validity concerns [1]. Our experiment situates itself within this literature: we test a canonical GVR pipeline in a closed‑loop, emulation‑grounded setting and report exact, archived evidence so that the null outcome can be interpreted against the preregistered estimand and execution contract.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration, estimand, and mapping: We preregistered the full design (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01). The primary estimand is the absolute paired difference in unsafe‑apply rate: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline = (guarded_unsafe_rate − baseline_unsafe_rate), where unsafe_apply = 1 and safe_apply = 0. The archived execution artifacts use a 'success' field that records safe outcomes; to avoid confusion we explicitly map archived names to the preregistered estimand here: archived 'baseline_success_count = 240' corresponds to baseline safe_apply = 240 (baseline unsafe_apply = 0). The registered analysis executor paired_binary_analysis_v1 computed the paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) and bootstrap CI (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl).

Design and sampling: N = 240 distinct tasks executed as paired episodes (baseline LLM‑only vs guarded GVR) with task composition: in‑distribution 60% (144), distribution‑shift 20% (48), adversarial 20% (48). Tasks were generated deterministically by a benchmark task generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) per the preregistration. Generation semantics and adapter contract: the registered adapter (hosted_netops_gvr_v1) used shared_initial_candidate semantics: exactly one initial LLM generation was produced per task and reused for both arms; the guarded arm could invoke at most one validator‑triggered repair per task. This execution contract was preregistered and constrains estimand interpretation: the guarded arm can only change paired outcomes if the shared initial candidate fails the deterministic validator or if a repair is applied.

Model, validator, and runtime budget: declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini" (execution/model_configuration.json). The validator used was deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator checks described in archived validator traces). Repair budget per guarded task was at most one repair call. Planned_episode_count = 480 (240 pairs × 2), maximum_model_calls = 480, preregistered retry policy allowed up to two infra‑recovery attempts; primary analysis treatment excludes unrecoverable infra failures (none occurred).

Scoring and analysis: Each final configuration was deterministically scored safe (0) or unsafe (1) by the validator and emulator oracle. The paired_binary_analysis_v1 executor produced the paired contingency table, 95% bootstrap percentile CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729), and an exact two‑sided McNemar test on discordant pairs. All per‑episode metadata, provider traces, validator traces, and analysis artifacts were archived (see execution_manifest and analysis artifacts referenced below).
sections.results:
Execution accounting: The adapter completed the run as registered: planned_episode_count = 480, completed_episode_count = 480, complete_pair_count = 240; hosted_model_call_event_count = 240 (shared initial generation), model_calls_used = 240 (execution_manifest). No infra failures occurred.

Primary binary outcomes and inference: Every episode was scored safe under both arms. Summary (analysis/condition_summary.csv): baseline successes = 240, baseline failures = 0 (baseline unsafe_apply = 0); guarded successes = 240, guarded failures = 0 (guarded unsafe_apply = 0). Paired contingency (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv): n11 = 240 (both safe), n10 = 0 (guarded unsafe & baseline safe), n01 = 0 (baseline unsafe & guarded safe), n00 = 0 (both unsafe). The paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00; bootstrap 95% percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (bootstrap_resamples = 10,000; seed = 1729 recorded in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. The analysis artifacts and exact numeric outputs are archived at analysis/results.json and accompanying CSVs.

Validator and repair activity: No validator‑triggered repairs were applied in any guarded episode (repair_attempts = 0 across archived repair logs). Consequently every guarded final configuration equaled the shared initial candidate and matched the baseline final configuration. Representative per‑task validator traces (e.g., execution/scoring/task-000004-guarded.json) show validator validation_before and validation_after metadata (difficulty pattern, required_command_count, normalized_configuration) and record validator PASS semantics and the lack of repair prompts.

Missingness and contamination: analysis/missingness_summary.csv and analysis/contamination_summary.csv report zero infra failures, zero unscorable episodes, and zero 'possible false‑safe' flags; therefore no preregistered exclusions affected the primary analysis. Deterministic reconciliation artifacts confirm accounting consistency (deterministic_reconciliation.json: all_deterministic_consistency_checks_passed = true).
sections.discussion:
Null paired outcome interpretation: The preregistered H1 (GVR reduces unsafe‑apply rate compared to LLM‑only) is not supported by these data. The null result is artifact‑grounded and arises from two execution facts: (1) shared_initial_candidate semantics produced one shared LLM output per task that was reused across arms, and (2) deterministic_netops_validator_v5 passed every shared initial candidate, so the guarded pipeline had no occasion to apply repairs or alter any paired outcome. Under these conditions the paired contrast is degenerate (no discordant pairs) and the paired estimate is exactly zero with a collapsed bootstrap CI.

Statistical diagnostics and interpretation: When n10 = n01 = 0 the McNemar statistic is degenerate and p = 1.0; the bootstrap CI collapses to a point mass at zero because all resamples reproduce identical concordant outcomes. The analysis executor's bootstrap parameters (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) and outputs are archived and confirm the numeric claims. This behavior correctly reflects the observed data and is not an analysis error; rather it highlights a design constraint that made the paired contrast uninformative for measuring verifier benefit in this execution.

Design lessons and artifact‑grounded recommendations: The archive contains specific, artifact‑backed recommendations to produce informative paired contrasts in future runs: (A) relax shared_initial_candidate semantics to permit independent initial generations per arm or otherwise permit generator variability between arms so validators have opportunities to detect candidate failures; (B) increase repair search budget and permit multi‑iteration repairs so that repair logic can be exercised when validator failures occur; (C) broaden adversary sampling beyond a single fixed attacker seed to probe more adaptive prompt injections; (D) expand deterministic verifier semantic coverage and instrument routine cross‑checks between validator PASS and emulator outcomes to detect potential false‑safe cases (the preregistered contamination checks were implemented and reported, producing zero flags in this run). Each recommendation is directly grounded in archived artifacts (execution_manifest, analysis/contamination_summary.csv, representative validator traces).

Threats to validity: Internal validity is limited by the shared_initial_candidate semantics and single‑model execution (gpt‑5‑mini). Construct validity is limited by the deterministic_netops_validator_v5 rule coverage (some semantic fault classes remain unmodeled). External validity is limited by the benchmark corpus (NetConfArena‑style synthetic tasks) and single‑provider model scope. Conclusion validity is constrained because baseline unsafe rate = 0 rendered the paired contrast untestable—future experimental designs should anticipate generator variability or increase adversarial difficulty to produce informative discordant pairs. All these threats and recommendations are traceable to archived execution artifacts.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, paired, emulation‑grounded evaluation of a generate–validate–repair pipeline for LLM‑based configuration generation. Observed outcomes: every paired episode was safe under both arms, yielding paired difference = 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00,0.00]; McNemar p = 1.0). Deterministic reconciliation confirms that no validator‑triggered repairs occurred because the single shared initial candidate passed the deterministic validator in every task. Critically, under preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics the guarded arm can only affect paired outcomes when the shared initial candidate failed validation or when a repair was applied; we state this constraint explicitly to avoid implying that the paired contrast measured an independent effect of constrained prompting or generator variability. We archive the preregistration, execution manifest, per‑call traces, validator traces, and analysis artifacts to enable follow‑up experiments that vary generation semantics, adversary strength, or verifier coverage. Future paired studies should permit generator variability between arms or increase repair/search budgets to produce informative discordant pairs and thereby measure verifier benefit empirically.

disclosure_statement: Models and orchestration: The experiment used a single hosted model (declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini") via the registered adapter hosted_netops_gvr_v1. The guarded pipeline used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and permitted up to one validator‑triggered repair per task. Runtime sampling: archived execution/model_configuration.json records temperature = null (unset); unset temperature does not imply deterministic sampling by the hosted provider and sampling nondeterminism remains possible; all model‑call metadata were archived. Preregistration and autonomy: the study was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01; preregistration SHA‑256: 3e73ca0dc935a8754bf2dfbe6869ff989c47f1db0d93e2ca34809be8ebf95e26) and executed under the frozen plan after the autonomy lock; a human Research Director selected the broad topic family and constrained the initial master prompt prior to the lock; no manual human editing of the technical manuscript content occurred post‑lock. Preregistered generation semantics: the registered adapter used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one shared initial generation per task reused across both arms), so only validator‑triggered repairs could create paired divergences; this semantics is explicitly used and reported in Methods and Results. Execution accounting (archived): planned_episode_count = 480, completed_episode_count = 480, complete_pair_count = 240, hosted_model_call_event_count = 240, model_calls_used = 240. Immutable master prompt: the initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Reproducibility pointer: archived execution manifest, per‑call traces, task manifests, validator traces, and analysis artifacts are available in the execution bundle (execution/execution_manifest.json and analysis/).
limitations: Emulator and corpus scope: tasks used a NetConfArena‑style synthetic emulation corpus; external validity to production, multi‑vendor networks and operator workflows is limited.
Single model: a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) was tested; results do not imply generality across models, prompt templates, or prompting strategies.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired design used one shared initial generation per task; this prevents generator variability between arms and makes verifier benefit contingent on initial candidates failing validation.
Adversary bounds: adversarial prompts were generated under a preregistered, fixed attacker protocol and do not represent unconstrained, adaptive adversaries.

Verifier coverage: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implements a finite set of checks; uncovered semantic fault classes may remain undetected by the verifier, and verifier PASS vs simulator outcome mismatches were planned to be flagged and analyzed (none occurred in this run).
